ORANGE.summary: Balance orange with navy, grey, denim or blue so it reads bold, not loud.

RUST.summary: Rust is a warm autumn tone that looks best with navy, brown, olive and cream.

rules.title: Start from a neutral
rules.text: Build on a neutral base, then add one bold colour. Neutrals let a statement colour do the talking without clashing.

rules.title: About three colours
rules.text: Most outfits look best with around three colours. Shades of one colour count once, and a fourth works when it is deliberate.

rules.title: Balance 60-30-10
rules.text: Give roughly 60% of the outfit to a main colour, 30% to a second and 10% to an accent. Avoid splitting colours evenly.

rules.title: Tonal dressing
rules.text: Wear several shades of one colour head to toe. Vary lightness and texture, such as knit with leather, so it never looks flat.

rules.title: Neighbours are easy
rules.text: Colours that sit next to each other on the colour wheel look related and calm. The closer they sit, the easier they are to pair.

rules.title: Handle opposites with care
rules.text: Opposite colours give maximum contrast. Mute or deepen at least one, or anchor the pair with a neutral, rather than wearing two pure hues.

rules.title: Navy and black
rules.text: Navy and black can be worn together. Keep the navy clearly blue, vary the textures and add a lighter third colour to separate them.

rules.title: Black and brown
rules.text: Black and brown is no longer a faux pas. Let one colour lead, mix textures such as leather and knit, and avoid matching depths that blur.

rules.title: Denim is a neutral
rules.text: Blue denim behaves like a neutral and pairs with almost anything, especially white, camel, navy, brown and red.

rules.title: Denim on denim
rules.text: Double denim looks sharpest when the washes match closely or clearly contrast. Break it up with a white or striped top.

rules.title: Mixing metals
rules.text: Gold and silver can be worn together. Let one metal lead, or start with a piece that combines both, and keep the style consistent.

rules.title: Metallics as neutrals
rules.text: Gold and silver behave like neutrals. A metallic bag, shoe or piece of jewellery is an easy way to break up a one-colour outfit.

rules.title: White all year
rules.text: The no-white-after-summer rule is an old etiquette relic. Wear white all year; let fabric set the season, with linen for summer and wool for winter.

rules.title: Match your contrast
rules.text: Echo your own colouring: high contrast between hair and skin suits bold pairings, while low contrast suits softer, muted ones.

rules.title: Avoid near-misses
rules.text: Two shades that almost match look like a mistake. Either match them exactly or make the difference obvious.

rules.title: One bright at a time
rules.text: Two loud colours of equal weight compete. Let one bright lead and keep the rest neutral, unless the clash is fully deliberate.

rules.title: Dress for the season
rules.text: Pastels and brights suit spring and summer; deeper earth and jewel tones such as burgundy, rust and forest green suit autumn and winter.

rules.title: Start colour small
rules.text: New to colour? Introduce it in an accessory first, then a shirt or knit, then larger pieces like trousers and coats.

rules.title: Pastels need light partners
rules.text: Pastels look freshest with white, cream, beige or grey. Black can swallow them and make the look heavy.

rules.title: Patterns count
rules.text: A pattern brings its colours into the count. Repeat one of its colours elsewhere in the outfit to tie everything together.

styleRules.title: Fitted with relaxed
styleRules.text: Balance volume: pair a relaxed piece with a fitted one. Wide trousers want a neat top; a slouchy knit wants slim legs.

styleRules.title: Cropped meets high-rise
styleRules.text: A cropped top or jacket should meet a high waistband, so no gap breaks the line and the legs look longer.

styleRules.title: Show the waist with wide legs
styleRules.text: With wide-leg trousers, tuck or crop the top so the waist shows; volume on volume swamps the frame.

styleRules.title: The third piece
styleRules.text: Top and bottom make clothes; a third piece makes an outfit. Add a blazer, cardigan, overshirt or a scarf to finish.

styleRules.title: Oversized over slim
styleRules.text: An oversized blazer or knit looks deliberate over slim trousers or leggings, not over equally baggy bottoms.

styleRules.title: Match jacket length to skirt
styleRules.text: A cropped blazer suits a skirt with a defined waist; an oversized blazer suits a fuller, longer skirt.

styleRules.title: Full skirt, slim top
styleRules.text: Balance a full midi skirt with a slim, fine-knit top and a sleek shoe to keep the shape clean.

styleRules.title: Lengthen long hems
styleRules.text: Maxi dresses and long wide-leg trousers look less swamping with a pointed toe or a little height.

styleRules.title: Blend to lengthen
styleRules.text: Match an under-layer to your trousers to lengthen the legs, or to your top to lengthen the torso.

styleRules.title: Mind the trouser break
styleRules.text: Slim trousers look sharpest with little or no break; a slight break is the most versatile, from loafers to sneakers.

styleRules.title: Let the hem pick the shoe
styleRules.text: Puddling wide legs need a heel or chunky sole; cropped hems let flats, sandals and loafers show.

styleRules.title: Room for layers
styleRules.text: Outer layers need room for what's beneath but shouldn't be oversized. If it won't button over your layers, it's too small.

styleRules.title: Jumpsuit length and waist
styleRules.text: A jumpsuit should reach the ankle and sit in at the waist; add a belt if a loose one swallows your shape.

styleRules.title: Hoodie under tailoring
styleRules.text: Under a blazer, keep the hoodie plain and trim, roomy but not sloppy, with sleeves ending at the wrist.

styleRules.title: Match shoe to formality
styleRules.text: Match the shoe to the outfit's formality: lace-ups for tailoring, loafers for smart casual, sneakers and sandals for casual.

styleRules.title: Sneakers with suits, done right
styleRules.text: Clean, low-profile leather sneakers now sit fine under a suit for smart-casual events. Keep runners and chunky soles out of it.

styleRules.title: Formal codes stay formal
styleRules.text: Where an invitation says black tie or business formal, wear proper leather shoes. Sneakers suit relaxed or unstated codes only.

styleRules.title: White sneakers go furthest
styleRules.text: White or cream sneakers suit almost any suit colour; black sneakers with a dark suit can look schoolboyish.

styleRules.title: Shorter shorts, lighter shoes
styleRules.text: The shorter the shorts, the more casual the shoe: sneakers and sandals for short hems, loafers for knee-length tailored shorts.

styleRules.title: No heavy shoes with shorts
styleRules.text: Boots and black dress shoes look heavy with shorts. Choose loafers, espadrilles, sneakers or sandals instead.

styleRules.title: Loafers like a narrow hem
styleRules.text: Loafers look best with tapered or cropped legs; a wide opening covers the low vamp and makes feet look stubby.

styleRules.title: Brown suede for denim
styleRules.text: Brown suede is the easiest leather with jeans. Sleek black shoes suit black or grey denim better than indigo.

styleRules.title: Sneakers with dresses
styleRules.text: Pick the sneaker to suit the dress: slim retro runners for crisp cottons, chunkier pairs for minis and slips.

styleRules.title: Socks follow trousers
styleRules.text: Match socks to trousers rather than shoes; when the ankle shows, the leg looks longer and the outfit calmer.

styleRules.title: When to go no-show
styleRules.text: No-show socks suit loafers, boat shoes and sneakers with shorts or cropped trousers. Keep them away from dress shoes.

styleRules.title: Sports socks for sport
styleRules.text: White athletic socks belong with athletic shoes only.

styleRules.title: One pattern leads
styleRules.text: Let one pattern lead and keep the others quiet; a busy pattern beside another busy pattern fights.

styleRules.title: Vary the scale
styleRules.text: When mixing two patterns, make one large and one small so each reads clearly.

styleRules.title: Share a colour
styleRules.text: Mixed prints should share at least one colour and a similar intensity; a bright print beside a muted one looks accidental.

styleRules.title: Stripes act as neutrals
styleRules.text: Fine stripes behave almost like a solid, which makes them the easiest pattern to add to a print.

styleRules.title: Same pattern twice
styleRules.text: Stripe on stripe or check on check works only when the scales are clearly different; similar sizes shimmer.

styleRules.title: Use a solid bridge
styleRules.text: A solid piece between two patterns calms the mix. When in doubt, add a plain layer.

styleRules.title: Animal print as a neutral
styleRules.text: Animal print can act as a neutral with solids and stripes; pair it with one other print at most.

styleRules.title: Contrast your textures
styleRules.text: Pair opposites: smooth with rough, matte with shine. Silk with knit, or leather with wool, adds depth to a plain palette.

styleRules.title: Texture rescues tonal outfits
styleRules.text: In a one-colour or neutral outfit, vary fabrics and weaves so the look doesn't fall flat.

styleRules.title: Keep a shared colour story
styleRules.text: Textured pieces work best in a shared colour family, so the texture reads rather than the clash.

styleRules.title: Fabric follows the season
styleRules.text: Linen, seersucker and light cotton for summer; tweed, flannel, corduroy and heavier wool for winter.

styleRules.title: Match knit to shirt weight
styleRules.text: Pair fine-gauge knits with crisp, smooth shirts, and chunkier knits with sturdier oxford, denim or flannel.

styleRules.title: Thin to thick
styleRules.text: Layer from thin to thick: the lightest fabric next to the body, the heaviest on the outside.

styleRules.title: Three visible layers
styleRules.text: Three visible layers is the sweet spot; a fourth usually tips into bulk. An undershirt doesn't count.

styleRules.title: Every layer stands alone
styleRules.text: Each layer should look good on its own, so the outfit still works when the coat comes off.

styleRules.title: Light inside, dark outside
styleRules.text: Lighter colours inside and darker ones outside is a reliable starting point, not a fixed law.

styleRules.title: Shirt cuff and collar under knits
styleRules.text: Under a jumper, let a few millimetres of shirt cuff show and keep the collar points inside the neckline.

styleRules.title: Layering a slip dress
styleRules.text: Wear a fine tee or thin knit under a slip dress, and a blazer or leather jacket over it for structure.

styleRules.title: Gilet for smart warmth
styleRules.text: A slim padded gilet fits under a blazer or coat for warmth without bulky sleeves.

styleRules.title: Hoodies under tailoring
styleRules.text: A plain hoodie under a blazer or overcoat is now an accepted high-low look for relaxed offices and weekends.

styleRules.title: Hem shape decides
styleRules.text: Straight hems are made to be worn out; long curved tails are made to be tucked.

styleRules.title: Untucked length
styleRules.text: Worn untucked, a shirt should end around mid-fly. Any longer and it needs tucking.

styleRules.title: Tuck under tailoring
styleRules.text: Tuck any shirt worn under a blazer or waistcoat. Under a jumper, tuck for smart looks; with jeans, an inch of tail can show.

styleRules.title: The front tuck
styleRules.text: A front or French tuck defines the waist of a loose tee or knit without a full tuck's formality; it suits mid to high rises.

styleRules.title: Occasion beats hem
styleRules.text: When the hem and the occasion disagree, the occasion wins: tuck for weddings, interviews and smart dinners.

styleRules.title: Polos by bottom
styleRules.text: Tuck a polo into tailored trousers or chinos; with jeans or shorts, wear it out or half-tucked.

styleRules.title: Contrast your washes
styleRules.text: For double denim, keep washes a couple of shades apart, usually darker on the bottom.

styleRules.title: Or commit to one wash
styleRules.text: A fully matching wash reads as a deliberate set; a near-miss looks accidental.

styleRules.title: Break up the blue
styleRules.text: A white tee or striped knit between two denim pieces stops double denim looking heavy.

styleRules.title: Vary the fit
styleRules.text: In double denim, vary the fits: relaxed jeans with a neat jacket, slim jeans with a boxy one.

styleRules.title: Jeans under a blazer
styleRules.text: With a blazer, choose dark, clean, straight jeans with no rips, and keep them darker than the jacket.

styleRules.title: Belt matches shoes
styleRules.text: Keep belt and shoes in the same colour family and finish: brown with brown, suede with suede.

styleRules.title: Don't mix black and brown
styleRules.text: Avoid mixing black and brown leathers in one outfit unless it is clearly intentional.

styleRules.title: Match your hardware
styleRules.text: Match the belt buckle to your watch and other hardware: silver with silver, gold with gold.

styleRules.title: Mixed metals in jewellery
styleRules.text: Mixing gold and silver jewellery is now accepted; it looks intended when the pieces are stacked or layered together.

styleRules.title: Casual relaxes the rules
styleRules.text: Leather and metal matching matters most with tailoring. With sneakers and casual clothes, a canvas or braided belt is fine.

styleRules.title: Belt width
styleRules.text: A dress belt about 3 cm wide suits tailoring; wider, chunkier belts belong with jeans.

styleRules.title: The knit tie
styleRules.text: A knit tie is the casual tie: wear it with oxford shirts, tweed or cotton jackets and dark jeans, not sleek business suits.

styleRules.title: Ties and jumpers
styleRules.text: A tie works under a V-neck or open cardigan; under a crew neck the knot disappears.

styleRules.title: Backpacks and suits
styleRules.text: Backpacks suit blazer-and-jeans looks. With a full suit, carry a structured bag so straps don't crush the shoulders.

styleRules.title: High-low done right
styleRules.text: High-low works when one piece breaks the formality and the rest stays sharp: clean sneakers, a pressed tee, a well-cut suit.

styleRules.title: A suit jacket is not a blazer
styleRules.text: A smooth suit jacket worn alone with jeans looks like half a suit; choose a textured jacket instead.

styleRules.title: Coats for tailoring
styleRules.text: Over tailoring, a wool overcoat, topcoat or trench is the classic choice; parkas and puffers dress a suit down.

styleRules.title: Puffers with suits
styleRules.text: If a puffer must go with tailoring, choose a slim, dark, hoodless one, or wear a gilet under the jacket.

styleRules.title: Cargo has a ceiling
styleRules.text: Cargo trousers can look smart but never formal; skip dress shirts, ties and sleek dress shoes with them.

styleRules.title: Evening means evening shoes
styleRules.text: Evening dress calls for evening shoes, such as heels, and a small evening bag like a clutch. Trainers and flip-flops break the code.

LOUNGE.summary: Home days, slow weekends and quick errands: soft, easy pieces that still look put-together if someone knocks.
tips: Treat loungewear as a set: a matching soft top and jogger looks intentional, not slept in.
Choose fibres that breathe all day: cotton jersey, merino or cashmere beat stiff, clingy synthetics.
Retire stretched, bobbled or stained pieces to sleep only; keep a few you'd happily answer the door in.
A cardigan or zip hoodie is the easiest layer for a cool house; slip-on trainers make errands painless.

ACTIVE.summary: Workouts, runs, hikes and sport: technical, sweat-wicking layers and the right shoe for the activity come before looks.
tips: Pick sweat-wicking synthetics or merino over cotton, which stays wet and chills you when you stop.
Match the shoe to the sport: running shoes for road, hiking boots off-road, flat trainers for lifting.
Start slightly cool. You warm up within minutes, so wear thin layers you can unzip or tie off.
In cold or wind, add a light shell over a base layer rather than one thick jumper.
Outdoors in strong sun, add a cap, sunglasses and a light long-sleeve top.

CASUAL.summary: Weekends, coffee, errands and relaxed plans: comfortable, clean pieces with one considered detail.
tips: Casual still means clean and well-fitting: no holes, stains or slogans, nothing you'd only wear at home.
Lift a tee and jeans with one considered piece: an overshirt, a good knit or leather shoes.
Dark, unripped denim works almost anywhere casual; keep shorts for warm days and relaxed plans.
Pick shoes you can walk in all day; a casual day out rarely goes exactly to plan.

WORK.summary: Most offices now run on business casual: tailored trousers or dark jeans, a shirt or fine knit, and a blazer for meetings. Go a notch smarter for clients.
tips: Ties and full suits are now for court, boardrooms and big pitches; most offices sit at business casual.
Keep a blazer or smart cardigan at your desk to lift a knit or polo for an unplanned client call.
Minimal leather trainers pass in many offices; scuffed running shoes don't. Loafers are the safe middle.
Meeting clients or unsure? Dress a notch above your team; a jacket is easier to remove than to find.
Offices swing between chilly air-con and warm rooms, so build in a knit or cardigan you can take off.

SMART.summary: Good restaurants, theatre, cocktail parties and client dinners: polished separates or a dress, a jacket, and proper shoes.
tips: Smart casual is the catch-all: tailored trousers or a skirt, a shirt or fine knit, and a jacket.
Evening in town needs more polish than a country lunch: go darker, add a jacket, swap trainers for leather.
Many upscale restaurants enforce dress codes; athletic wear, beachwear, caps and flip-flops get refused.
Denim is risky at smart evening events; dark tailored trousers are the safer bet.
Cocktail means dressy but not black tie: a dark suit or velvet jacket, a cocktail dress or evening separates.

DATE.summary: From coffee to a tasting menu: match the venue, wear something you love and can move in, and add one personal detail.
tips: Match the venue: jeans and a good top for coffee or a bar; a dress or tailored trousers for a smart dinner.
Wear something you've worn before; new shoes or a top that rides up means fidgeting all evening.
Choose shoes you can walk in for hours; the plan often moves on to a second place.
Add one personal note, like your most complimented colour or a great jacket, not a head-to-toe trend.

FORMAL.summary: Weddings, galas, black-tie dinners and ceremonies: follow the invitation's dress code to the letter, and when unsure, dress up.
tips: The invitation is the brief: black tie, lounge suits and cocktail each mean something specific.
Overdressing beats underdressing; if the wording is vague, choose the dressier reading.
After 6pm go darker and richer: velvet, satin, silk. Daytime calls for lighter colours and fabrics.
Check the ground: grass, sand and cobbles call for block heels, flats or loafers, not stilettos.
At weddings, skip anything that could read as bridal white unless the couple asks for it.

TRAVEL.summary: Flights, trains and long drives: soft, breathable layers, an easy waist, slip-on shoes, and your bulkiest coat worn rather than packed.
tips: Cabins swing hot and cold: a breathable base plus a knit or cardigan; a big scarf doubles as a blanket.
Choose stretch and easy waists for long sits; stiff denim and tight fits pinch after a few hours.
Slip-on shoes speed up security and cope with swollen feet; wear your bulkiest pair to save space.
Skip lint magnets like fleece and corduroy on planes, and keep jewellery and belts minimal.
Dress your outer layer for the destination's weather and pack a fresh top in your hand luggage.

dressCodes.name: Casual
dressCodes.summary: Relaxed and comfortable but clean and intentional: jeans or chinos with a tee, polo or casual shirt, and trainers or sandals. Nothing ripped, stained or slogan-led.

dressCodes.name: Come as you are / Relaxed
dressCodes.summary: Hosts mean everyday clothes, not loungewear: your best casual pieces, clean and pressed, with shoes you can stand in.

dressCodes.name: Dressy casual
dressCodes.summary: A step above casual for nicer dinners, fundraisers and after-work events: a dress, or smart trousers with a good top; blazer optional, denim only if dark and sharp.

dressCodes.name: Smart casual
dressCodes.summary: The everyday catch-all: chinos or tailored trousers with an open-neck shirt or fine knit and a jacket, or a dress or skirt. Polished shoes; denim depends on the venue.

dressCodes.name: Business casual
dressCodes.summary: Today's office default: tailored trousers, chinos or dark unripped jeans with a shirt, blouse, knitted polo or fine knit. Blazer optional, tie rare; loafers or minimal leather trainers.

dressCodes.name: Business professional / Business formal
dressCodes.summary: For boardrooms, court, finance and big pitches: a matching dark suit or a dress with jacket, a collared shirt or blouse, a tie where expected, and polished leather shoes.

dressCodes.name: Creative / Start-up office
dressCodes.summary: Personal style is welcome: dark jeans or wide-leg trousers, a tee or knit under an overshirt or unstructured jacket, clean trainers. Polished, never gym-ready.

dressCodes.name: Interview
dressCodes.summary: Dress one level above the company's everyday code: a suit for business-casual firms, tailored trousers or chinos with a blazer for casual ones. Neat, muted and well fitting.

dressCodes.name: Cocktail
dressCodes.summary: Dressy and glamorous, a step below black tie: a dark suit or velvet jacket (tie optional), a cocktail dress, dressy jumpsuit or evening separates, and heels or polished shoes.

dressCodes.name: Semi-formal
dressCodes.summary: Between business and cocktail: a dark suit with tie, or a knee-to-midi afternoon or cocktail dress or dressy separates. After 6pm, lean dressier.

dressCodes.name: Festive / Holiday party
dressCodes.summary: Cocktail-level with a seasonal twist: velvet, satin, a little sparkle or a rich colour; a blazer in a festive shade or a party dress.

dressCodes.name: Garden party / Daytime wedding
dressCodes.summary: Smart daywear outdoors: a light suit or linen blazer with an open-neck shirt, or a midi or tea-length day dress, often with a hat. Pick heels that won't sink into grass.

dressCodes.name: Beach wedding / Beach formal
dressCodes.summary: Special-occasion but sand-friendly: linen or cotton suiting and shirts, flowing midi or maxi dresses, light colours, and flat sandals, espadrilles or loafers.

dressCodes.name: Lounge suits
dressCodes.summary: Despite the name, this means business-smart: a dark or grey suit with collar and tie, or a dress with jacket or a skirt or trouser suit, and polished shoes. Common on wedding invitations.

dressCodes.name: Morning dress
dressCodes.summary: Formal daywear for weddings, royal garden parties and race days: a morning coat, waistcoat and striped trousers, or a formal day dress with a hat. Never after 6pm.

dressCodes.name: Black tie optional
dressCodes.summary: Formal evening wear is welcome but not required: a dinner suit, or a dark suit with white shirt and dark tie; a floor-length gown, formal midi or evening-fabric cocktail dress.

dressCodes.name: Black tie
dressCodes.summary: The classic formal evening code: a black or midnight dinner jacket with silk lapels, matching trousers, white shirt and black bow tie, or an evening dress, long or dressy cocktail length.

dressCodes.name: Creative black tie
dressCodes.summary: Black tie with personality: a velvet or coloured dinner jacket, a patterned bow tie, statement waistcoat or regular tie; dramatic evening dresses or sharp evening trousers.

dressCodes.name: White tie
dressCodes.summary: The most formal code, always spelled out on the invitation: black tailcoat, wing-collar shirt, white waistcoat and bow tie, or a full-length evening gown; long gloves optional.

dressCodes.name: Dress to impress / Glamorous
dressCodes.summary: The hosts want everyone dressed up: cocktail-plus, with statement fabrics like velvet, satin or sequins and your sharpest shoes. Under-dressing isn't an option.

dressCodes.name: Festival
dressCodes.summary: Comfort and weatherproofing first: tees and shorts or jeans, a hoodie or fleece for night, a packable waterproof, a hat, and boots or wellies you can stand in all day.

dressCodes.name: Athleisure
dressCodes.summary: Sport-derived comfort worn off-duty: clean leggings or joggers, a sweatshirt or zip hoodie and sleek trainers, finished with a structured coat or blazer so it looks intentional.

weather.title: Severe cold
weather.advice: Layer properly: thermal base, wool or fleece mid-layer and an insulated hooded coat. Cover head, hands and face; bare skin chills fast.

weather.title: Freezing
weather.advice: Wear a warm knit under a padded or heavy wool coat, plus hat, gloves and scarf. Boots with grip for icy pavements.

weather.title: Cold
weather.advice: A wool coat or puffer over a jumper does the work. Add a scarf and gloves, and keep feet in closed shoes or boots.

weather.title: Chilly
weather.advice: Time for a proper coat or a lined jacket over knitwear. Trousers or jeans rather than bare legs, and a scarf for the walk.

weather.title: Cool
weather.advice: Classic in-between weather: a trench, denim or leather jacket over a long-sleeve layer, with closed shoes.

weather.title: Mild
weather.advice: One light layer is enough: a cardigan, overshirt or unlined blazer over a tee or shirt that you can shed by afternoon.

weather.title: Warm
weather.advice: Short sleeves in breathable cotton or linen. Keep a light layer to hand for air-con or the evening.

weather.title: Hot
weather.advice: Go loose and light: linen and cotton, open shoes and sunglasses. Skip layers you'd only end up carrying.

weather.title: Very hot
weather.advice: Dress for airflow: loose, light-coloured linen or cotton that covers your shoulders, a brimmed hat and sandals. Stay in shade at midday.

weather.title: Rain
weather.advice: Wear a hooded waterproof and shoes that can handle puddles. Leave suede and jute soles at home; dark trousers hide splashes.

weather.title: Cold rain
weather.advice: Wet layers lose their warmth fast, so put a waterproof over a wool or fleece layer and wear sealed boots and gloves.

weather.title: Heavy, stormy rain
weather.advice: Umbrellas struggle in this wind. A fully waterproof hooded jacket and rain boots work better; keep hems clear of puddles.

weather.title: Warm showers
weather.advice: Warm rain calls for a light, packable waterproof, not a coat. Quick-drying fabrics and rubber soles beat suede and canvas.

weather.title: Snow
weather.advice: Grip and dry feet first: insulated, treaded boots, then a warm coat, hat and gloves. Keep hems over or tucked into boots.

weather.title: Strong wind
weather.advice: A close-fitting windproof shell beats a loose coat. Skip wide brims and floaty hems; a beanie and scarf stay put.

weather.title: High UV
weather.advice: Cover up: a brimmed hat, UV-blocking sunglasses and closely woven fabric over your shoulders. Sunscreen on anything still bare.

weather.title: Very high UV
weather.advice: Limit direct sun from 11 to 3. Long, loose sleeves in tightly woven fabric, a wide brim and wraparound sunglasses.

weather.title: Hot and humid
weather.advice: Sweat can't evaporate, so wear loose linen, seersucker or light cotton. Skip clingy synthetics, heavy denim and extra layers.

weather.title: Cool start, warm afternoon
weather.advice: Build the outfit from layers you can remove, and choose a jacket light enough to carry once it warms up.

fabrics.tip: Breathable and easy, but it holds sweat and dries slowly. Swap it for wool or synthetics in cold, wet or sporty weather.
fabrics.care: Wash at 30-40C; line-dry or tumble low to limit shrinking. Iron while slightly damp.

fabrics.tip: The hot-weather hero: cool to the touch, quick-drying and strong. Creases are part of the charm, so choose easy cuts.
fabrics.care: Wash 30-40C, line-dry and iron damp. Softens with each wash; avoid sharp repeated folds.

fabrics.tip: Warm even when damp and naturally crease- and odour-resistant. Air it between wears rather than washing each time.
fabrics.care: Air between wears; wool cycle or cool hand-wash, dry flat. Store clean against moths.

fabrics.tip: Fine, soft wool that regulates temperature and resists odour: ideal for base layers, travel tees and office knits.
fabrics.care: Wool cycle at 30C or hand-wash; dry flat. Airing refreshes it between washes.

fabrics.tip: Light, very soft and warm for its weight. Some pilling is normal; fine-gauge knits layer neatly under a coat or blazer.
fabrics.care: Hand-wash lukewarm or 30C delicate; never wring or tumble. Fold, don't hang.

fabrics.tip: Warmer than sheep's wool, light, and almost lanolin-free, so it rarely itches. Made for chunky knits and scarves.
fabrics.care: Hand-wash cool with wool wash, press water out in a towel and dry flat. Fold to store.

fabrics.tip: Lustrous, resilient and crease-resistant. Fluffy mohair knits are light winter warmers; mohair-blend tailoring stays crisp in summer.
fabrics.care: Hand-wash cool and dry flat; brush gently to lift the halo. Dry-clean tailoring.

fabrics.tip: Hard-wearing cotton twill for most casual plans. Heavy denim is hot in summer and stays wet for hours once soaked.
fabrics.care: Wash rarely, inside out and cold, to keep the colour; line-dry. New dark denim can bleed.

fabrics.tip: Looks like denim but is a lighter plain weave, so it breathes like a shirt. A smart-casual staple under a blazer.
fabrics.care: Machine-wash 30-40C, hang to dry and iron while damp.

fabrics.tip: Ridged cotton pile that traps warmth. Wide wale reads chunky and casual; fine needlecord is smarter and layers easily.
fabrics.care: Wash inside out and cool; never iron the pile flat. Brush to lift it once dry.

fabrics.tip: Soft brushed cloth. Cotton flannel shirts are cosy casual layers; wool flannel trousers are the warm, smart office pick.
fabrics.care: Cotton: wash cool, tumble low. Wool flannel: air, brush and dry-clean sparingly.

fabrics.tip: Dense, rugged wool that shrugs off wind and light showers. Pair with knits, cords and boots for a country-smart look.
fabrics.care: Let mud dry then brush off; air out, steam creases and dry-clean rarely.

fabrics.tip: Puckered stripes hold the fabric off your skin so air moves through, and creases barely show. Brilliant for travel.
fabrics.care: Machine-wash cool and line-dry. No ironing needed; the pucker is woven in.

fabrics.tip: Blocks wind and ages with character. A leather jacket suits cool, dry days but isn't warm enough alone in deep cold.
fabrics.care: Wipe clean and condition a few times a year; let wet leather dry slowly, away from heat.

fabrics.tip: Soft napped leather that marks easily with water, salt and oil. Proof it before wearing and save it for dry days.
fabrics.care: Spray with protector; brush one way once dry; lift marks with a suede eraser. Never machine-wash.

fabrics.tip: Light, breathable and cool to the touch, yet it insulates under layers. Sweat and water can mark it, so keep it for dressier days.
fabrics.care: Hand-wash cold with gentle detergent or dry-clean; dry flat out of sun; iron cool inside out.

fabrics.tip: A weave, not a fibre: glossy and fluid in silk or polyester. Made for evening, but it snags easily and shows water marks.
fabrics.care: Hand-wash or dry-clean; steam, or iron cool through a cloth.

fabrics.tip: Dense pile that glows in evening light: the go-to for parties and winter formal. Sitting crushes it, so steam to revive.
fabrics.care: Dry-clean or follow the label; steam from the back, never iron the pile; hang, don't fold.

fabrics.tip: Stretchy knit that moves with you and packs without creasing. Thin jersey clings, so size up slightly or layer it.
fabrics.care: Wash cool and dry flat or low; fold rather than hang so it keeps its shape.

fabrics.tip: Tough, quick-drying and crease-resistant, so it's great for sport and travel. It traps heat and odour in humid weather.
fabrics.care: Wash cool without softener; tumble low. It sheds microfibres, so a wash bag helps.

fabrics.tip: Strong, light and quick-drying: the backbone of windbreakers and packable shells. Feels clammy against skin in heat.
fabrics.care: Wash cool and line-dry; keep away from high heat and irons.

fabrics.tip: Light, warm and quick-drying, but wind cuts straight through it. Wear it as a mid-layer under a shell on breezy days.
fabrics.care: Wash cool inside out, no softener; air-dry. Brush high-pile fleece to stop matting.

fabrics.tip: The warmest insulation for its weight, but it clumps and stops insulating when soaked. Add a shell over it in rain.
fabrics.care: Wash rarely with down wash; tumble low with dryer balls until fully dry to restore loft.

fabrics.tip: Not quite as warm for its weight as down, but it keeps insulating when damp, which makes it the better pick for wet cold.
fabrics.care: Machine-wash cool, tumble low until fully dry; store uncompressed.

fabrics.tip: Keeps rain out while letting sweat vapour escape. If water stops beading, the outer finish needs reviving, not a new jacket.
fabrics.care: Technical wash, no softener; tumble warm about 20 minutes to revive the water-repellent finish.

fabrics.tip: Fluid, cool and absorbent with a lovely drape, so it suits humid heat. It's weaker when wet and creases easily.
fabrics.care: Hand-wash cold or dry-clean; don't wring. Dry flat and iron low, inside out.

fabrics.tip: Wood-based fibres that feel silky, breathe and absorb moisture well; sturdier wet than viscose. Lovely for tees and dresses.
fabrics.care: Wash cool on gentle; line-dry or tumble low; iron low.

fabrics.tip: A budget stand-in for wool: soft and colourfast, but it pills quickly and loses warmth once wet.
fabrics.care: Wash cool and dry flat; heat can stretch it out of shape. De-pill with a fabric shaver.

fabrics.tip: Chunky and cable knits trap air for real warmth but need a roomier coat. Fine-gauge knits slip neatly under jackets.
fabrics.care: Fold, never hang. Wash gently for the fibre, dry flat and ease back into shape.

fabrics.tip: Open-weave, high-twist wool for summer tailoring: breathes almost like linen but sheds creases far better.
fabrics.care: Hang to air between wears and steam out creases; dry-clean rarely.

fabrics.tip: A coated fabric with a leather look. It doesn't breathe, so it gets sweaty indoors, and the coating can crack with age.
fabrics.care: Wipe with a damp cloth; keep away from heat and solvents. Machine-wash only if labelled.

fabrics.tip: Wax-coated cotton that shrugs off showers and wind and softens with wear. Ideal for drizzly city and country days.
fabrics.care: Never wash or dry-clean. Sponge with cold water and re-wax once a year.

trends.name: Chocolate brown and powder blue
trends.summary: Pale sky blue lifts deep chocolate brown. It walked in London and is the season's easiest colour contrast.
trends.howToWear: A pale blue shirt or jumper under a chocolate coat, or brown cords with a sky-blue knit.

trends.name: Chocolate brown as the new neutral
trends.summary: Chocolate was the most-used runway colour after black for autumn and now does the job of black or navy.
trends.howToWear: Swap black for brown: brown trousers or a suede jacket with cream knits, denim and tan boots.

trends.name: Royal purple
trends.summary: Royal purple and aubergine are the bright of the season, from chunky knits to sharp tailoring.
trends.howToWear: Start with one purple jumper over navy or brown trousers; mohair or suede keeps it relaxed.

trends.name: Purple and chocolate
trends.summary: Stylists ground the season's purple with chocolate instead of black for a richer, softer contrast.
trends.howToWear: A purple knit with chocolate wide-leg trousers, or a plum shirt under a brown blazer.

trends.name: Burgundy and oxblood
trends.summary: Burgundy was the most-used non-neutral on the autumn runways and a defining street-style shade.
trends.howToWear: Treat it as a neutral: a burgundy jumper with denim, or burgundy loafers and bag with grey or camel.

trends.name: Cobalt and electric blue
trends.summary: Saturated cobalt is autumn's sharpest bright and runs into 2027, when forecasters back a vivid luminous blue.
trends.howToWear: One cobalt jumper with ecru or mid-blue jeans; for more punch, add brown or burgundy.

trends.name: Cobalt and chocolate
trends.summary: Vivid blue against deep brown is the season's confident clash, warm and cool at once.
trends.howToWear: Pull a cobalt knit over brown trousers, or wear a brown coat with a blue jumper or scarf.

trends.name: Poppy red
trends.summary: A bright, orange-leaning red takes over from wine shades as the accent that pops against dark winter fabrics.
trends.howToWear: A red jumper tied over the shoulders with indigo jeans, or red socks with black loafers.

trends.name: Red and purple
trends.summary: Red worn with purple is the bold clash stylists took from the autumn runways.
trends.howToWear: A red knit with purple trousers, or keep it small with a purple scarf on a red coat.

trends.name: Mustard yellow
trends.summary: Mustard climbed sharply in autumn runway colour counts, used as the accent against browns and blues.
trends.howToWear: A mustard jumper or scarf with navy, cobalt or chocolate pieces; keep everything else plain.

trends.name: Burnt olive
trends.summary: A deep, muted olive works as a neutral this autumn and sits in the colour forecasters' winter palette.
trends.howToWear: Swap black trousers or a black coat for olive, then add cream, camel, chocolate or navy.

trends.name: Fuchsia accents
trends.summary: Punchy fuchsia cuts through the earthy autumn palette and carries into 2027, when forecasters back a vivid pink.
trends.howToWear: One pink piece only: a fuchsia knit with chocolate trousers, or a pink bag with navy.

trends.name: Tonal grey
trends.summary: Head-to-toe grey in mixed shades and textures is the quiet power look; charcoal rose on the Paris runways.
trends.howToWear: Charcoal roll-neck, grey pleated trousers and a grey coat; vary the textures and keep shoes dark.

trends.name: Relaxed grey suiting
trends.summary: Roomy, 1990s-style grey suits came back across the autumn shows, worn easy rather than sharp.
trends.howToWear: A grey blazer and trousers with a plain tee and trainers, or split them up with jeans.

trends.name: Leopard as a neutral
trends.summary: Leopard is worn like a neutral, from coats to bags, and spring keeps animal print tone-on-tone.
trends.howToWear: One leopard piece, a coat, scarf or flats, with denim and black or brown basics.

trends.name: Playful checks and plaid
trends.summary: Checks are the season's most wearable print, now looser, bigger and layered rather than strictly heritage.
trends.howToWear: A checked shirt or overshirt worn open over a knit, or check trousers with a plain jumper.

trends.name: Dark florals
trends.summary: Florals turn moody for winter, set on black grounds and worked into knits and jacquards.
trends.howToWear: A dark floral blouse or dress with a black knit, opaque tights and boots.

trends.name: Polka dots
trends.summary: Dots in every size are back on runways and in street style, on dresses, shirts and scarves.
trends.howToWear: A spotted scarf or shirt with denim and a plain coat; one dotted piece is enough.

trends.name: Velvet by day
trends.summary: Velvet returns for day as well as night, in tailoring, skirts and relaxed separates.
trends.howToWear: A velvet blazer over a T-shirt and jeans, or velvet trousers with a chunky knit.

trends.name: Suede in warm browns
trends.summary: Suede in tan, chestnut and chocolate leads the season's textures, from jackets to boots and bags.
trends.howToWear: A suede jacket over a grey hoodie or knit with straight jeans and boots.

trends.name: Leather beyond the jacket
trends.summary: Leather moves into trousers, skirts, shirts and long coats and is one of autumn's most-used runway fabrics.
trends.howToWear: Leather trousers or a leather skirt with a fine knit and loafers; one leather piece per outfit.

trends.name: Faux fur and shearling coats
trends.summary: Statement faux fur, shearling and calf-hair coats are the headline outerwear, often oversized or belted.
trends.howToWear: Throw a faux fur or shearling coat over jeans, a roll-neck and ankle boots.

trends.name: Bombers and flight jackets
trends.summary: Oversized leather bombers and shearling-collared flight jackets lead casual outerwear into spring.
trends.howToWear: A bomber over a knit with straight jeans, or with a midi skirt and boots.

trends.name: Funnel necks and high collars
trends.summary: Necklines rise: funnel necks, roll-necks and high collars replace plunging lines for autumn.
trends.howToWear: A fine roll-neck under a blazer or coat with the collar turned up; tuck it into trousers.

trends.name: Cinched-waist tailoring
trends.summary: Jackets nip in at the waist with peplums, wraps and belts, and spring keeps the defined waist.
trends.howToWear: Belt a blazer over a shirt or fine knit and wear it with straight trousers or jeans.

trends.name: The skirt suit
trends.summary: The matching skirt suit is back, from sharp pencil skirts to relaxed cuts, and spring pairs knee skirts with jackets.
trends.howToWear: A blazer with a matching skirt, knee boots and a fine knit; or split them and wear each with jeans.

trends.name: Tailored trousers
trends.summary: Tailored trousers were the most-shown key item for autumn, still rising, and stay core for spring.
trends.howToWear: Pressed trousers with a knit and trainers for weekdays, or with a shirt and loafers.

trends.name: Wide-leg tailoring for winter
trends.summary: Wide-leg trousers rose in Paris for autumn; spring shows narrow the line, so this is their last big season.
trends.howToWear: Wide-leg trousers with a tucked-in knit and a short jacket; finish with loafers or boots.

trends.name: Pea coats and sailor details
trends.summary: Nautical codes, pea coats, sailor collars and toggles, came through in luxe autumn fabrics.
trends.howToWear: A navy double-breasted coat over a striped top, jeans and loafers.

trends.name: Shirt and tie
trends.summary: Ties return as a styling accent with shirts and suits, and spring loosens them into belts and sashes.
trends.howToWear: A loosened skinny tie with a shirt and knit, or a tie threaded through jean belt loops.

trends.name: Knee-high and Western boots
trends.summary: Tall leather boots, Western suede pairs and lace-up knee boots lead the season's footwear.
trends.howToWear: Knee boots under a midi skirt or over straight jeans; Western boots with denim.

trends.name: Ballet flats
trends.summary: Ballet flats stay among the most-wanted shoes in shopping data and on the street.
trends.howToWear: Flats with straight jeans and a trench, or with tailored trousers and a fine knit.

trends.name: Slim retro trainers
trends.summary: Low-profile retro court and skate trainers ranked among the hottest products of the quarter.
trends.howToWear: Slim trainers with tailored trousers or a skirt, or with straight jeans and a long coat.

trends.name: Cardigan as a jacket
trends.summary: Chunky and cashmere cardigans are worn as the outer layer, buttoned over shirts and tees.
trends.howToWear: Button a chunky cardigan over a T-shirt, add trousers or jeans and skip the coat on mild days.

trends.name: Shirt under a sweater vest
trends.summary: School-uniform layering returns: shrunken or patterned vests over collared shirts, often with a tie.
trends.howToWear: A knitted vest over a crisp shirt with jeans or tailored trousers; let the collar show.

trends.name: Mixed textures, one palette
trends.summary: Street style's key trick: suede, leather, knits and faux fur layered within one colour family.
trends.howToWear: Keep to browns or greys and mix a cable knit, a suede jacket and leather boots.

trends.name: Scarves everywhere
trends.summary: The scarf is the go-to finish, at the neck, knotted at the waist or tied onto a bag.
trends.howToWear: Knot a silk scarf at the neck with a shirt, or tie one through the belt loops of jeans.

trends.name: Statement gloves
trends.summary: Gloves become the accent: leather or brightly coloured pairs finish coats and suits.
trends.howToWear: Bright leather gloves with a neutral coat, or match gloves to a scarf or trousers.

trends.name: Newsboy caps and berets
trends.summary: Looks are finished from the top: newsboy caps, berets, silk kerchiefs and pillbox hats.
trends.howToWear: A newsboy cap or beret with a long coat and jeans, or a silk scarf tied under the chin.

trends.name: Gold and silver metallics
trends.summary: Gold lamé and metallic accents marked autumn, and the spring shows push gold and silver into daywear.
trends.howToWear: A metallic skirt with a grey sweatshirt or plain knit, or silver shoes with denim.

trends.name: Big statement jewellery
trends.summary: Oversized gold jewellery, chunky bracelets worn over sleeves and bold necklaces lead accessories.
trends.howToWear: Stack a chunky bracelet over a coat cuff, or wear a bold necklace over a plain knit.

trends.name: Sleek rain slickers
trends.summary: Rain slickers get sharper cuts and glossy technical finishes, and utility macs rise in tailoring collections.
trends.howToWear: A glossy raincoat over a knit and tailored trousers, with boots or loafers.

trends.name: Slimmer trousers creep back
trends.summary: After years of wide legs, slim trousers, stirrups and skinny jeans are back on runways; shops follow slowly.
trends.howToWear: Try slim trousers with a long cardigan or an oversized coat to balance the line.

trends.name: Brown jeans
trends.summary: Searches for brown jeans are growing faster than for blue or black as warmer washes reach the runway.
trends.howToWear: Brown jeans with a cream knit and loafers, or a pale blue shirt for the brown-and-blue pairing.

trends.name: Jeans with a blazer
trends.summary: Paris paired relaxed straight jeans with tailoring; wool suiting appeared in nearly a quarter of denim looks.
trends.howToWear: A tailored blazer over a tee or shirt with straight-leg jeans and loafers or flats.

trends.name: Chartreuse and lime accents
trends.summary: Sharp chartreuse and lime are the accent colour from autumn into spring, used in small doses.
trends.howToWear: Show a chartreuse top under a jacket, or add lime shoes or a bag to navy and khaki.

trends.name: Orange and citrus
trends.summary: Orange is spring's new bright, from citrus shirt dresses to skirts, and forecasters back an energetic orange.
trends.howToWear: An orange shirt or skirt with white and denim, or one orange accessory with navy.

trends.name: Every shade of green
trends.summary: Green ran through all four fashion capitals for spring, from emerald to mint, worn almost as a neutral.
trends.howToWear: A green skirt or shirt with grey, white or denim; mix two greens for a tonal look.

trends.name: Mint and lavender
trends.summary: Spring pastels are layered together rather than worn alone, and mint with lavender is the key pairing.
trends.howToWear: A mint shirt with lavender trousers or a lavender knit; keep everything else white or grey.

trends.name: Soft pink and pistachio
trends.summary: Pistachio and mint paired with soft rose pink featured across the spring collections.
trends.howToWear: A pale pink shirt with a mint skirt or trousers; white trainers keep it fresh.

trends.name: Butter yellow and lilac
trends.summary: Pale butter yellow returns for spring, paired with lilac or sage for a soft colour story.
trends.howToWear: A pale yellow knit with lavender trousers, or a yellow shirt with white jeans.

trends.name: Powder blue
trends.summary: Powder blue rose into the top ten runway colours for spring in both New York and Milan.
trends.howToWear: A powder blue shirt or knit with white jeans or grey tailored trousers.

trends.name: Tonal whites
trends.summary: White was the fastest-rising runway colour for spring, worn head to toe with ecru and cream.
trends.howToWear: White jeans with a cream knit or shirt; vary the textures and add tan sandals or flats.

trends.name: White jeans
trends.summary: Searches for white jeans are climbing and the spring shows dress them up as statement trousers.
trends.howToWear: White jeans with a navy knit or striped shirt, or with a blazer and loafers.

trends.name: Double denim
trends.summary: Head-to-toe denim in matching washes was a defining spring look, often tailored or sold as sets.
trends.howToWear: A denim jacket with jeans in the same wash, a white tee and loafers or boots.

trends.name: The skirt is back
trends.summary: Skirts jumped from a fifth to over a quarter of spring runway looks; straight and midi lengths led.
trends.howToWear: A straight midi skirt with a tee and trainers, or with a bomber or blazer and flats.

trends.name: Trench as the outfit
trends.summary: Spring trenches are buttoned and belted as the whole outfit, with little showing beneath.
trends.howToWear: Belt a trench over a slip skirt or shorts so it reads as a dress, then add a strong shoe.

trends.name: Florals in full bloom
trends.summary: Florals are spring's top print and rising, now 3D, garlanded or embroidered as well as printed.
trends.howToWear: A floral skirt with a plain knit and trainers, or a floral shirt under a denim jacket.

trends.name: Stripes on stripes
trends.summary: Stripes are spring's second print and rose in New York, often clashed in more than one width.
trends.howToWear: A striped shirt with striped trousers in a different width; keep the colours in one family.

trends.name: Gingham and picnic checks
trends.summary: Checks move into spring as gingham, handkerchief checks and plaid prep separates.
trends.howToWear: A gingham shirt with white jeans, or a checked skirt with a plain tee.

trends.name: Polos and prep
trends.summary: Prep returns for spring: knit polos, rugby shirts, argyle knits and plaid separates.
trends.howToWear: A knit polo tucked into tailored trousers or a skirt, with loafers.

trends.name: Soft linen tailoring
trends.summary: Spring suiting goes soft and unstructured in linen, light cotton and silk blends.
trends.howToWear: A linen blazer with matching trousers and a tee, or split the suit and wear the jacket with jeans.

trends.name: Graphic and slogan tees
trends.summary: Playful graphics, slogans and poster prints return to tees, skirts and denim for spring.
trends.howToWear: A graphic tee under a blazer with a midi skirt or tailored trousers.

trends.name: Sleeveless tops
trends.summary: Sleeveless tops were the fastest-rising key item in Milan for spring, worn with skirts and tailoring.
trends.howToWear: A fine-knit or crisp sleeveless top tucked into a midi skirt or tailored trousers.

trends.name: Bubble and balloon volume
trends.summary: Bubble hems, balloon skirts and puffed shapes bring volume back for spring.
trends.howToWear: Balance a balloon skirt or puffed top with a fitted knit or slim trousers.

trends.name: Lowered waists
trends.summary: Waists drop: low-rise trousers, hip-slung skirts and dropped-waist dresses rose for spring.
trends.howToWear: Wear trousers or a skirt on the hips with a belt and a short knit or tucked-in tee.

trends.name: Lace and lingerie details
trends.summary: Lace, sheer blouses and lingerie-inspired details lead spring tops, and lace pieces are selling now.
trends.howToWear: A lace-trimmed cami under a blazer, or a sheer blouse over a plain vest with jeans.

trends.name: Hand-made knits
trends.summary: Knits with visible stitching, loose threads and hand-finished texture sell the human touch for spring.
trends.howToWear: A textured hand-knit over a slip skirt, or with relaxed jeans and loafers.

trends.name: Belts as the statement
trends.summary: Belts move centre stage for spring: doubled up, chain-trimmed or slung low on the hips.
trends.howToWear: A statement belt over a long knit or shirt dress, or two thin belts on jeans.

fading.name: All-beige quiet luxury
fading.summary: The beige-on-beige uniform is giving way to colour and ornament; beige fell in runway counts and buyers want joy.

fading.name: Palazzo and very loose trousers
fading.summary: Loose and palazzo trousers dropped hard on the spring runways as straight skirts and tailored trousers took over.

fading.name: Chinos as the default trouser
fading.summary: Chinos fell from about 7% to under 2% of spring runway looks; tailored wool trousers replace them.

fading.name: Mini dresses
fading.summary: Mini dresses halved on the spring runways as midi skirts, maxi dresses and dropped waists rose.

fading.name: Barrel-leg jeans
fading.summary: Searches peaked in April and have halved; the relaxed straight leg is now searched three times as often.

fading.name: Mom jeans and flares
fading.summary: Searches are falling (mom jeans down 10%, flares down 20%) as relaxed straight legs lead denim.

fading.name: Athleisure as an outfit
fading.summary: Streetwear's grip is loosening as tailoring and the defined waist return; keep joggers and hoodies for rest days.

fading.name: Cargo trousers
fading.summary: Years of saturation and the move to tailoring leave cargos looking dated outside of hiking and travel.

fading.name: Sheer-everything layering
fading.summary: Sheer looks fell on the Milan spring runway despite heavy press; lace and lingerie details replace full sheer.

classics.name: Trench coat
classics.summary: Fits every season's story, from autumn utility to spring's trench-as-dress, and works over anything.

classics.name: Navy blazer
classics.summary: The blazer is a top runway key item every season; navy dresses up jeans and down tailoring.

classics.name: Tailored trousers
classics.summary: The most-shown key item for autumn and still core for spring; a good pair outlasts every leg-width cycle.

classics.name: Straight mid-blue jeans
classics.summary: Fits shift between barrel, flare and skinny, but the straight leg in mid-blue is denim's steady centre.

classics.name: Crisp white shirt
classics.summary: Poplin keeps rising on the runway; a white shirt layers under knits and suits all year.

classics.name: Fine knit and roll-neck
classics.summary: Crew-necks and roll-necks in merino or cashmere anchor every autumn, whatever the trend colour.

classics.name: Camel coat
classics.summary: Camel stays in the top runway colours season after season, and a wool coat in it goes over everything.

classics.name: White leather trainers
classics.summary: Clean, low trainers keep topping shopping charts; they suit tailoring as easily as denim.

classics.name: Loafers
classics.summary: Loafers bridge smart and casual and return on runways season after season in new shapes.

classics.name: Breton stripe top
classics.summary: Stripes rank among the top three runway prints every season; the navy-and-white stripe never dates.

classics.name: Leather jacket
classics.summary: Leather is one of the most-used runway fabrics; a plain black or brown jacket adds edge for decades.

classics.name: Denim jacket
classics.summary: Worn as a trucker over knits in winter and as double denim in spring, it suits every season.

classics.name: Black dress
classics.summary: Black is the runway's number-one colour every season; a simple black dress goes from desk to dinner.

classics.name: Cashmere cardigan
classics.summary: Works as a layer or a light jacket and returns every autumn, whether chunky or fine.

classics.name: Ankle and Chelsea boots
classics.summary: Sleek ankle boots finish jeans, trousers and dresses alike, whatever the season's statement boot.

classics.name: White T-shirt
classics.summary: The base under blazers, knits and denim; even the most pared-back runways build on it.

classics.name: Ballet flats
classics.summary: A decades-old shape that keeps returning to the top of shopping charts.

classics.name: Simple watch
classics.summary: A slim classic watch made the hottest-products list for the first time in years; it never dates.

colourOfTheYear.name: Cloud Dancer (11-4201)
colourOfTheYear.summary: A soft, airy white and the first white ever picked; a calm base for crisp shirts, knits and tonal white looks.

colourOfTheYear.name: Transformative Teal
colourOfTheYear.summary: A blend of dark blue and aquatic green; a deep teal knit or coat is an easy way to wear it.

colourOfTheYear.summary: A vivid lapis-to-cobalt blue heading the spring 2027 palette with orange, pink, green and clay.

tips.text: A capsule wardrobe is a small set of pieces that all work together. One popular challenge allows 33 items, shoes and accessories included, for three months.
Build your capsule from what you already own. Pick favourites first, then list the real gaps before buying anything.
Refresh your capsule each season and store out-of-season pieces, so the rail only shows what works right now.
Plan around your actual week: list work days, weekends and events, then check each has an outfit before you shop.
The classic capsule is a few timeless staples, such as trousers, a knit and a coat, topped up with a handful of seasonal pieces.
Leave underwear, sleepwear, loungewear and gym kit out of your capsule count. Count what you actually get dressed in.
Try ten pieces for ten days, shoes and jackets included. It shows how many outfits you can make from very little.
Box up what's outside your capsule instead of giving it away at once. If you don't miss it in three months, let it go.
Small capsule recipe: four pieces in one neutral, four in a second, four that mix both and four in an accent colour.
A capsule works because it sets a limit. Choose a size that suits your life and hold it for a full season.
Across your closet, aim for roughly 60–70% neutrals, 20–30% secondary colours and up to 10% bold accent.
Two or three neutrals are enough for a base. Navy, grey, camel, cream or black: pick the ones you reach for most.
Choose one or two accent colours and repeat each in at least two pieces, so an accent can anchor a whole outfit.
Keep shoes, belts and bags in the same neutral family and your outfits will look intentional with no effort.
Tonal dressing is easy: pair shades that sit side by side, such as camel with brown or grey with charcoal.
For crisp contrast, pair neutrals from opposite ends of the scale, such as navy with cream or black with white.
Put your accent colour into easy-to-swap pieces like a scarf or top, so one neutral outfit can look new each day.
Solid pieces are the easiest to pair. Keep prints to a minority and wear each one with solids.
Too many accent colours make it feel as if nothing goes. Two or three you love beat eight you only like.
Build around two neutrals and almost every top works with every bottom. That is the secret of a small closet.
Mix-and-match maths: 5 tops and 3 bottoms give 15 outfits. Add 2 layers, worn or not, and you reach 45.
Before adding a top, name three things you'd wear it with. Stylists plan about three tops for every bottom.
One cardigan or overshirt over five tops gives five new outfits. Plan about one layer for every three tops.
Accessories refresh a repeat outfit fastest. Swap the scarf, belt or bag and the same pieces look new.
A blazer is the hardest-working layer: over a T-shirt at the weekend, over a shirt for work.
A dress or jumpsuit is a whole outfit in one piece. Change the shoes and layer to take it from day to evening.
Shoes set the formality: the same jeans and knit read casual with sneakers and smart with loafers.
Pieces that roll over between seasons, like knits, jeans and shirts, form the backbone of a capsule.
Write down outfit formulas that work, such as shirt, trousers and loafers, then repeat them with different pieces.
Repeating outfits is good style. Wearing favourites often is exactly what makes a closet work.
Wash at 30°C instead of 40°C: tests found it saves around 38% of the energy per load.
Fill the drum. A few full loads use less energy than daily small washes.
Wash denim less. Wearing jeans ten times between washes cuts their water and climate impact by around 75%.
Line-dry instead of tumble drying. A lifecycle study of jeans found it cut energy use and climate impact by around two-thirds.
Turn the dial down: the same jeans study found a cold wash cut climate impact by about a quarter.
Washing and care make up about a third of clothing's carbon footprint, so how you wash matters as much as what you buy.
Give leather shoes 24 hours' rest between wears so sweat can dry and the leather keeps its shape.
Slip cedar shoe trees in within an hour of taking shoes off; they draw out moisture and prevent creasing.
Rotate at least two pairs of everyday shoes. Each lasts longer when it gets a day off.
Sew a loose button back on straight away. Nearly three in four people feel confident doing it, and it rescues a favourite.
Learn one repair a season. Only about a third of people feel able to take up a hem or darn a hole, yet both are quick to learn.
Tackle stains straight away rather than writing pieces off; most people already know how to remove them.
Clean the dryer filter after every load: a blocked filter can use 50% more energy on the last load.
Take zips, pockets and resizing to an alterations shop. Few people feel able to do them at home, and repair beats replacing.
Air jeans and jackets between wears instead of washing after every outing. Less washing means a longer life.
Before buying, ask: will I wear this at least 30 times? If not, leave it on the rail.
Shop from a list, not a mood. Note the gaps in your closet and buy only what fills them.
Shop a few planned times a year rather than every week. Planning ahead takes the impulse out of buying.
Buy for the life you have: if most days are work days, most of your closet should be work-ready.
Check seams, fabric weight and finish before buying. Durable pieces lower your cost per wear over time.
Look second-hand first. Buying pre-loved keeps clothes in use and avoids much of the footprint of making new ones.
Hire or borrow for one-off events. Hiring and repairing keep clothes in active use for longer, saving carbon and water.
A discount isn't a bargain if the piece never gets worn. Judge sale buys on cost per wear, not on the saving.
Poor fit is the main reason clothes go unworn. If it doesn't fit well in the shop, it won't fit better at home.
Four in five people own clothes they don't wear because they no longer fit or need altering. A tailor can fix most.
Having trousers hemmed to the right length is a quick, low-cost alteration that makes a piece look made for you.
Keep clothes that fit you now. Pieces saved for 'one day' take up space and rarely get worn.
Leave taking in or letting out to an alterations specialist; only about one in eight people feel able to do it.
Fit beats price. A piece that fits gets worn, and wear is what brings the cost per wear down.
Cost per wear is price divided by wears. A £120 coat worn 120 times costs £1 a wear.
A cheap top worn three times can cost more per wear than a better one worn fifty times.
Set separate cost-per-wear goals for everyday and occasion pieces; event outfits will always cost more per wear.
Save ahead for a seasonal clothing budget so purchases are planned rather than impulsive.
Unworn clothes are money sitting idle: UK households own about £4,000 of clothing, and 30% goes unworn for a year.
Washing at 30°C instead of 40°C can save around £24 a year for a household running four washes a week.
Spend more on long-life pieces such as coats, knits and jeans; they're the garments where durability pays most.
Repair before replacing: a new zip or hem costs a fraction of a new garment and keeps a favourite in use.
Between 2000 and 2015 the number of times a garment was worn fell by 36%, while clothing production doubled.
Less than 1% of the material used to make clothing is recycled into new clothing. Wearing things longer matters more.
Every second, the equivalent of a rubbish truck of textiles is landfilled or burned somewhere in the world.
Keeping half of the UK's clothes in use nine months longer would cut their carbon by 8% and water by 10%.
UK clothes last about 3.3 years on average. Every extra season of wear trims their footprint.
Since 2000, shoppers have bought about 60% more garments a year but kept them only half as long.
In one national survey, 40% of the clothes in people's wardrobes were rarely or never worn.
The 80/20 rule of thumb: most people wear about 20% of their clothes 80% of the time. Log your wears to find your 20%.
The EU generates around 16 kg of textile waste per person a year, and less than a third is collected separately.
Pass on what you don't wear. Resale or donation gives clothes a second life and keeps them out of the bin.
One UK survey found new clothes were worn only around seven times on average. Aim for at least 30.
Clothes shed microfibres in the wash; about half a million tonnes reach the ocean each year. Wash less, in full loads.
Pack about three tops for every bottom. Bottoms can be worn several times between washes; tops can't.
Try 5-4-3-2-1 packing: five tops, four bottoms, three pairs of shoes, two swimsuits and one hat. Adjust for the trip.
Start with two or three neutral bottoms and four to six light tops, then add only what the trip demands.
Pack shoes that suit everything in the case. If a pair works with only one outfit, leave it at home.
A 16-piece capsule built from two neutrals and one accent colour fits in a carry-on and mixes endlessly.
Keep every piece in your travel palette, so any top goes with any bottom and nothing travels as a one-off.

checks.title: Palette needs a neutral base
checks.message: Only {value} of your closet is neutral, so pieces are harder to pair. Mix-and-match closets sit nearer 60–70%.
checks.action: Add basics in navy, grey, white or camel that go with your colours.

checks.title: Mostly neutrals
checks.message: Your closet is {value} neutrals. A few more pieces in one accent colour would add life without breaking the mix.
checks.action: Pick one accent you love and repeat it in two or three pieces.

checks.title: Too many accent colours
checks.message: {value} different accent colours are competing. Outfits pair more easily when one to three colours repeat.
checks.action: Favour your top two or three accents when you next shop.

checks.title: Focused colour palette
checks.message: Two accent colours on a neutral base: a tight palette where almost everything pairs.
checks.action: Repeat each accent in a top, a layer or an accessory.

checks.title: Well-balanced palette
checks.message: Three accent colours give you variety while keeping outfits easy to mix.
checks.action: Keep new buys within these three accents and your neutrals.

checks.title: Prints are competing
checks.message: {value} of your pieces are bold patterns. Prints clash easily, so you need solids to do the pairing.
checks.action: Pair each print with solids and make your next buy a plain piece.

checks.title: Easy-pairing solids
checks.message: Only {value} of your closet is boldly patterned, so nearly every piece pairs with every other.
checks.action: Add one print you love to lift the solids.

checks.title: Bigger than you need
checks.message: {value} pieces is far beyond the 33 a three-month capsule uses. Surveys find much of a big closet sits unworn.
checks.action: Try a 33-piece capsule for three months and box up the rest.

checks.title: Capsule-sized closet
checks.message: {value} pieces is capsule territory: small enough to see at a glance, big enough for weeks of outfits.
checks.action: Keep it lean: one in, one out.

checks.title: Short on tops
checks.message: Your tops count is {value}. Capsules usually carry 8–15, so laundry day comes round fast.
checks.action: Add two or three easy tops in your core neutrals.

checks.title: Few bottoms
checks.message: Your bottoms count is {value}. Capsules usually carry 5–9 so every top has something to go with it.
checks.action: Add neutral trousers or jeans that suit most of your tops.

checks.title: Instant outfits ready
checks.message: {value} dresses, jumpsuits or other one-pieces: whole outfits in one go for busy mornings.
checks.action: Change the shoes and layer to take them from day to evening.

checks.title: Add a layer
checks.message: Your layering count is {value}. A knit or overshirt worn over your tops multiplies your outfits.
checks.action: Add a neutral cardigan, knit or overshirt that goes over most tops.

checks.title: Layers multiply outfits
checks.message: {value} layering pieces: each one turns the tops you already own into new outfits.
checks.action: Try each layer over a top you rarely wear.

checks.title: A lot of coats
checks.message: {value} coats and jackets is more than most climates need. One per type of weather usually covers it.
checks.action: Keep your best one per weather type and pass on the rest.

checks.title: Shoes need a rest day
checks.message: With only {value} in your shoe rotation, no pair gets the 24 hours it needs to dry out between wears.
checks.action: Aim for three pairs to rotate: casual, smart and weather-ready.

checks.title: Plenty of shoes
checks.message: {value} pairs of shoes is more than double the nine a typical seasonal capsule uses.
checks.action: Pass on pairs you haven't worn this year.

checks.title: No bag logged
checks.message: No bags in your closet yet. One neutral everyday bag finishes most outfits.
checks.action: Add the bag you carry most, or plan one in a neutral.

checks.title: No accessories
checks.message: No accessories yet. A belt, scarf or watch is the quickest way to change a repeat outfit.
checks.action: Add the accessories you own; a scarf in your accent colour is a good start.

checks.title: Accessories at work
checks.message: {value} accessories to change the look of the same core pieces, so repeat outfits never feel repeated.
checks.action: Restyle a favourite outfit with a different accessory this week.

checks.title: Tops are thin on the ground
checks.message: You have {value} tops per bottom. Tops do most of the work, and stylists plan two to three per bottom.
checks.action: Buy tops before bottoms until you reach two or three per bottom.

checks.title: Bottoms are overworked
checks.message: You have {value} tops per bottom, so your bottoms carry every outfit and will wear out first.
checks.action: Add one versatile bottom in a neutral.

checks.title: No rain-ready coat
checks.message: No waterproof coat yet. Wet days are the gap most closets leave, and one good coat closes it.
checks.action: Add a raincoat, trench coat or hooded parka.

checks.title: No warm coat
checks.message: None of your outerwear is rated warm. Coats are among the longest-lived clothes, so one good one pays back.
checks.action: Add one insulated coat, parka or puffer in a neutral.

checks.title: No smart shoes
checks.message: No smart shoes yet. Interviews, weddings and dinners all call for one polished pair.
checks.action: Add loafers, Chelsea boots or dress shoes in black or brown.

checks.title: Smart shoes covered
checks.message: {value} pairs of smart shoes: you're ready for dinners, interviews and dressier days.
checks.action: Rotate them and use shoe trees to keep their shape.

checks.title: Nothing for formal days
checks.message: Nothing in your closet reaches business level. One tailored piece covers interviews and events.
checks.action: Add a blazer or tailored trousers that also dress up jeans.

checks.title: Very casual closet
checks.message: {value} of your closet is casual. A few smart-casual pieces would stretch it to work, dinners and events.
checks.action: Make your next buy a shirt, knit polo or tailored trousers.

checks.title: Casual and smart in balance
checks.message: A healthy spread of casual and smarter pieces: you're dressed for most occasions.
checks.action: Mix one smart piece into a casual outfit to stretch both.

checks.title: Closet in active use
checks.message: You've worn {value} of your closet in the last 30 days. It's working hard.
checks.action: Keep logging wears to spot your true favourites.

checks.title: Much of the closet is resting
checks.message: Only {value} of your closet was worn in the last 90 days. Most people wear about 20% of their clothes 80% of the time.
checks.action: Style three unworn pieces this week, or move them on.

checks.title: Beating the 80/20 rule
checks.message: {value} of your closet was worn in the last 90 days, far better than the usual 80/20 pattern.
checks.action: Keep your buying this considered.

checks.title: Unworn pieces
checks.message: {value} of the pieces you've had over two months are still unworn. Poor fit is the usual reason.
checks.action: Wear each one this month, have it altered, or pass it on.

checks.title: Everything gets worn
checks.message: Every piece you've had for over two months has been worn. Nothing in your closet is idle.
checks.action: Keep shopping this way: only what you'll wear 30 times.

checks.title: High cost per wear
checks.message: Your average cost per wear is {value}. Wearing favourites more often is the fastest way to bring it down.
checks.action: Before buying, ask: will I wear this at least 30 times?

checks.title: Clothes earning their keep
checks.message: Your average cost per wear is just {value}. Your clothes are earning their keep.
checks.action: Keep caring for favourites so they last even longer.

checks.title: Few warm-weather pieces
checks.message: Your hot-weather count is just {value}. A heatwave would leave you short of cool options.
checks.action: Add breathable tops and a light bottom in linen or cotton.

checks.title: Few cold-weather pieces
checks.message: Your cold-weather count is just {value}. Winter needs knits and a warm layer.
checks.action: Add a warm knit and check you have a winter coat.

checks.title: Lots of lookalikes
checks.message: You own {value} pieces of the same type in the same colour. Near-duplicates split wear without adding outfits.
checks.action: Skip this type and colour next time; try a new shape or accent.

checks.title: Every piece adds something
checks.message: Little doubling-up: almost every piece brings a new colour or shape to your outfits.
checks.action: Keep checking new buys against what you own.

checks.title: Laundry pile-up
checks.message: {value} of your closet is in the wash. Many pieces can be aired and worn again before washing.
checks.action: Run a full load at 30°C, and air jeans and knits between wears.

checks.title: Long wishlist
checks.message: {value} pieces on your wishlist. A long list tends to turn into impulse buys.
checks.action: Run each through the 30-wears test and keep your top five.

ratios.summary: Stylists and published capsules land on two to three tops per bottom, just under one layer and one pair of shoes per bottom, and a small handful of coats.

essentials.name: Rain-ready coat
essentials.why: Wet days are the gap most closets leave. A trench or hooded coat keeps every outfit wearable.

essentials.name: Warm winter coat
essentials.why: Coats were the longest-lasting garment in a UK survey, at about 4.6 years, so a good warm coat pays back.

essentials.name: Light jacket
essentials.why: Covers mild days and the gaps between seasons, over almost any outfit.

essentials.name: Blazer
essentials.why: Dresses up jeans, smartens a T-shirt and handles interviews: the most versatile layer.

essentials.name: Neutral knit
essentials.why: One knit for every three tops multiplies outfits and carries you through the cooler months.

essentials.name: Plain T-shirts
essentials.why: Plain tees in white or a core neutral are the base of countless outfits and the piece editors wear most.

essentials.name: Crisp shirt
essentials.why: A plain shirt moves from desk to dinner and layers neatly under knits and blazers.

essentials.name: Dark jeans
essentials.why: Straight, dark denim goes with nearly every top and turns smart with a blazer.

essentials.name: Tailored trousers
essentials.why: Neutral trousers cover work, dinners and travel in a single piece.

essentials.name: Warm-weather bottom
essentials.why: A neat, light bottom keeps hot-weather outfits polished rather than beachy.

essentials.name: One-piece outfit
essentials.why: A whole outfit in one piece that dresses up or down with a change of shoes.

essentials.name: Clean sneakers
essentials.why: Minimal leather or canvas sneakers work with jeans, trousers and relaxed tailoring.

essentials.name: Smart shoes
essentials.why: Interviews, weddings and dinners need one polished pair in black or brown.

essentials.name: Weather-ready boots
essentials.why: Wet pavements ruin fabric shoes; a sealed leather or rubber boot keeps you going.

essentials.name: Summer sandals
essentials.why: Covers hot days and holidays when closed shoes feel heavy.

essentials.name: Everyday bag
essentials.why: One neutral bag that carries the daily essentials and suits most outfits.

essentials.name: Evening bag
essentials.why: A smaller, structured bag for dinners and events where a tote looks too casual.

essentials.name: Leather belt
essentials.why: Finishes tucked shirts and trousers; choose one in the same neutral family as your shoes.

essentials.name: Scarf
essentials.why: Adds warmth and colour, and changes a repeat outfit in seconds.
